_: Name, description and badge live in src/resources/connectors.json so the console and the browser process cannot disagree about them.

notes: OAuth 2 only. Basecamp's own authorization document mentions personal access tokens in passing, but nothing in the API reference says where a user creates one, so Flux does not offer that path - offering a field with no instructions is worse than not offering it.

The scope list is empty deliberately, not forgotten: Basecamp's authorize URL takes response_type, client_id and redirect_uri and no scope parameter. A Basecamp-issued token reports a scope back on the authorization document ("full"), but there is no documented way to ask for a narrower one, so the narrowing has to happen in Flux - which is what the write_scope on each operation below is for.
Register the app at launchpad.37signals.com/integrations to get client_id and client_secret.
The legacy type=web_server and type=refresh parameters still work but response_type=code and grant_type=refresh_token are the documented form.

token.note: Access tokens last two weeks. The token response always carries a refresh_token; POST grant_type=refresh_token with client_id and client_secret to the same token_url. A connector that does not refresh silently stops working a fortnight after the user connects it.

account_discovery.note: This is the mandatory first call after authorizing - it is where the base URL comes from. Pick the account whose "product" is "bc3" and use its "href" verbatim as the API base. Do not build https://3.basecampapi.com/{account_id} yourself; the href is the contract.
account_discovery.also: Basecamp serves its own copy at GET https://3.basecampapi.com/authorization.json (no account prefix). It omits identity name/email and replaces "product"/"app_href" with an RFC 8707 "resource" (urn:bc:account:{id}), so a client reading both must select accounts by href or resource and treat product as optional.

api.base_url_note: Templated only for documentation. At runtime it is the href from the authorization document - see auth.account_discovery.

pagination.request: Follow the URL in the RFC 5988 Link header with rel="next". Never construct a page URL.
pagination.response: A blank Link header is the last page. X-Total-Count carries the size of the whole collection.
pagination.note: Page size is geared, not fixed: 15 on page 1, 30 on page 2, 50 on page 3, 100 from page 4 on. Code that assumes a constant page size will miscount.

caching.note: Basecamp asks that clients use freshness headers, not as an optimisation but as a condition of use. Store the ETag and Last-Modified from every response and send them back as If-None-Match and If-Modified-Since; a 304 costs no bandwidth and no rate-limit goodwill.

errors.400: Almost always a missing or malformed User-Agent header. See gotchas.
errors.415: Content-Type was not application/json; charset=utf-8 on a POST or PUT.
errors.429: Read Retry-After (seconds) and wait exactly that long. Do not use a fixed backoff.
errors.404: Deleted content, insufficient permission, or an inactive account. Never retried automatically.
errors.404 with Reason: Account Inactive: The whole account is suspended or its trial expired. Every request to it will fail. Disable the connection in Flux and tell the user; retrying is pure noise.
errors.5xx: 500, 502, 503 and 504 are retryable with exponential backoff.

gotchas: The User-Agent header is mandatory and must name the app AND a way to contact its author. Without it every request is 400 Bad Request - not 401, not 403, which is why it reads like a bug in the request body.

Creating a message or a document WITHOUT a status field creates a draft, not a post. It notifies nobody and does not appear on the board. Pass status: "active" to publish. Schedule entries invert this: they publish immediately unless you pass status: "drafted".

Flat routes (/todos/{id}.json) are canonical. The /buckets/{project_id}/... form still works in perpetuity but is legacy. Three endpoint families are the exception and are still project-scoped only: message types (/buckets/{id}/categories.json), the webhooks index and create, and adding a tool to a dock.
bucket_id and project id are the same number. A project has exactly one bucket, so anywhere the docs say bucket, the project ID is the value.
Everything in a project is a "recording", which is why comments are posted to /recordings/{id}/comments.json regardless of whether the thing being commented on is a message, a to-do or an upload.

Check a project's dock before assuming a tool exists. Message boards, to-do sets, schedules and campfires can each be disabled per project, and the dock array in the project payload is what says which are enabled and what their IDs are.

The search endpoint's project filter is bucket_ids[] (plural, array). The recordings endpoint uses bucket. They are different parameter names for the same idea and swapping them silently returns unfiltered results.

Rich text is HTML with a fixed allowed tag set: div, h1, br, strong, em, strike, a (with href), pre, ol, ul, li and blockquote. Anything else is stripped silently, so content that looked right in the request comes back missing.
A to-do can live directly under the todoset, outside any list - the todoset payload counts them as completed_loose_todos_count. Walking only the to-do lists misses them.

get_authorization.notes: Absolute, not relative to base_url - this is the call that produces the base URL. Also returns expires_at, which is the cheapest way to know a token is about to lapse.

list_projects.notes: Active projects visible to the user, newest first. Each carries its dock, which is where the message_board, todoset, schedule and chat IDs come from.

get_todoset.notes: The todoset ID comes from the project's dock, not from a list endpoint.

list_todos.notes: Returns only active, pending to-dos by default. completed=true returns only completed ones; status=archived or status=trashed returns archived or trashed to-dos including both pending and completed. The two combine.

create_todo.notes: Requires content. Optional description (HTML), assignee_ids, completion_subscriber_ids, due_on, starts_on, and notify. Draft rather than send while notify is false: the to-do is visible in the project but nobody is messaged. Set notify true only under a send-scoped task.

draft_message.notes: Omit status. Requires subject; content is optional HTML. The message is created as a draft and notifies nobody, which is what makes this the draft-scoped form of the same endpoint as post_message.

post_message.notes: Same endpoint with status: "active". Publishes and notifies. Everyone on the project is notified and subscribed unless subscriptions is given as an array of person IDs.

publish_message.notes: Publishes an existing draft with a body of {"status": "active"} and nothing else. The update merges, so subject, content and subscribers are preserved - resending them is how you change who gets notified by accident. Documents publish the same way via PUT /documents/{id}.json.

create_comment.notes: Send, not draft: every subscriber to the recording is notified the moment it posts, and there is no draft state for a comment. Requires content as HTML.

create_campfire_line.notes: Requires content. Pass content_type: "text/html" for rich text; plain text is the default. A campfire line cannot be drafted, so this is always send.

get_my_assignments.notes: Grouped into priorities ("Up Next") and non_priorities. Card table steps are folded into their parent card as children.

get_assignments_due.notes: scope is one of overdue, due_today, due_tomorrow, due_later_this_week, due_next_week, due_later; defaults to overdue. An unrecognised scope is a 400 that lists the valid ones.

prioritize_assignment.notes: Adds a recording to Up Next. Returns 204 No Content - no body to parse.

create_schedule_entry.notes: Requires summary, starts_at and ends_at (ISO 8601). Send, not draft, because a schedule entry over the API publishes immediately unless status: "drafted" is passed - the opposite default to messages and documents. participant_ids, all_day, url (returned as join_url), highlighted, notify and recurrence_schedule are optional.

list_project_people.notes: The source of the person IDs that assignee_ids, subscriptions and participant_ids take.

get_my_profile.notes: The correct way to learn who the token belongs to inside Basecamp. The identity on the authorization document is a Basecamp ID, not a person, and the docs say plainly not to use it for this.

get_search_metadata.notes: Fetch this before searching rather than hardcoding type names - the docs say the available types vary. Keys look like Kanban::Card and Schedule::Entry, not "card" and "event".

search.notes: Requires q. Optional type_names[], bucket_ids[], creator_ids[], file_type, exclude_chat, since (last_7_days | last_30_days | last_90_days | last_12_months | forever), sort (best_match | recency), page, per_page. The singular type, bucket_id and creator_id are deprecated.

create_document.notes: Requires title and content (HTML). Draft-scoped because status is omitted; passing status: "active" publishes and notifies, which is a send-scoped act.

get_notifications.notes: Grouped into unreads, reads, memories, bubble_ups and scheduled_bubble_ups.

rate_limits.first_limit: 50 requests per 10 seconds per IP address, as of the docs' own wording ("currently").
rate_limits.note: Several limits run at once - separate ones for GET and POST, and per-second, per-hour and per-day windows - and Basecamp adjusts them dynamically. That makes a hardcoded client-side limiter wrong by design. Obey Retry-After on a 429 and treat backpressure as normal rather than exceptional.
rate_limits.retry: 429 carries Retry-After in seconds. 5xx is retried with exponential backoff. 404 is never retried.

webhooks.note: Available, and project-scoped only: GET and POST /buckets/{project_id}/webhooks.json, then GET, PUT and DELETE /webhooks/{id}.json. Not wired into Flux yet - the agent polls - so they are listed here rather than in operations.
webhooks.payload_url: Requires a publicly reachable URL, which a desktop browser does not have. This stays unimplemented until there is somewhere for Basecamp to POST to.

not_implemented.note: Basecamp has 50-plus resource types. What is above is the set a task can actually be built on; these are known, documented, and deliberately left out for now.

source.note: Read from a clone of basecamp/bc-api at commit a2899b2, which is Basecamp's own API reference, rather than from search results.
